# Estimation

An estimator is a statistic used as a guess at a parameter. The number it produces on the observed sample is the estimate. The two are written with the same symbol, and the distinction is whether the sample is still random. $\widehat\theta(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ has a sampling distribution. $\widehat\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is a number.

The families below are the ones on the [common distributions](../reference/distributions.qmd) page, reached through a [random sample](inf-01-statistical-inference.qmd#def-random-sample).

## Method of moments

::: {#def-method-of-moments .definition}
## Method of moments

Suppose the first $k$ population moments exist and determine $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k)$. The method of moments matches them to the corresponding sample moments and solves for $\theta$.

:::

For a single mean, the first moment gives $\widehat\mu=\overline X$. For a mean and a variance together, $\E X_i^2=\mu^2+\sigma^2$, so the second sample moment produces

$$
\widetilde\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\overline X)^2=\frac{n-1}{n}s^2.
$$

For independent Bernoulli trials with success probability $p$, the first moment is $p$ itself, so the moment estimator is the sample proportion $\overline X$. The same matching idea estimates a correlation by the sample correlation of the pairs $(X_i,Y_i)$.

Moment estimators are easy to write down and often consistent. They are not, in general, the estimators with the smallest variance.

## Maximum likelihood

::: {#def-maximum-likelihood .definition}
## Maximum likelihood

For a random sample with density or mass function $f(x;\theta)$, the likelihood is

$$
L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\theta).
$$

A maximum likelihood estimate is a value $\widehat\theta$ that maximises $L$. The maximum likelihood estimator is the same formula with the random sample in place of the observed numbers.

:::

The logarithm is strictly increasing, so $\log L$ has the same maximiser, and a sum is easier to differentiate than a product. For a scalar parameter the likelihood equation is $\partial\log L/\partial\theta=0$, provided the maximum is interior and the derivative exists. For a vector parameter there is one equation per coordinate.

A single $\Bin(n,p)$ count $X=x$ has log-likelihood $x\log p+(n-x)\log(1-p)$, up to a constant. Setting the derivative to zero gives $\widehat p=x/n$.

For $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ independent and $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$,

$$
\log L(\mu,\sigma^2)=-\frac1{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2-\frac n2\log\sigma^2,
$$

up to a constant. The likelihood equations return $\widehat\mu=\overline x$ and

$$
\widehat\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\overline x)^2.
$$

So the normal mean is estimated by the sample mean, and the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance divides by $n$, not by $n-1$.

The maximiser transforms with the parameter. If $\widehat\theta$ maximises $L$ and $g$ is a one-to-one reparameterisation, then $g(\widehat\theta)$ maximises the likelihood written in the new parameter. Estimating $\sigma$ by the square root of $\widehat\sigma^2$ is the case people use.

## Comparing estimators

::: {#def-unbiased-estimator .definition}
## Unbiased estimator

An estimator $T$ of $\theta$ is unbiased when $\E T=\theta$ for every $\theta$ in the parameter space. The bias is $\E T-\theta$.

:::

The sample mean is unbiased for $\mu$, by linearity, whenever the mean exists. The bias-corrected sample variance $s^2$ is unbiased for $\sigma^2$. The maximum likelihood estimator $\widehat\sigma^2=((n-1)/n)s^2$ has bias $-\sigma^2/n$. Unbiasedness is not free: removing that bias can raise the variance.

::: {#def-mean-squared-error .definition}
## Mean squared error

The mean squared error of an estimator $T$ of $\theta$ is $\E(T-\theta)^2$. It splits as

$$
\E(T-\theta)^2=\Var(T)+(\E T-\theta)^2.
$$

:::

The split is the variance–bias tradeoff. An estimator with a small bias can have a smaller mean squared error than an unbiased competitor, if the unbiased one is much more variable. One estimator is more efficient than another when its mean squared error is smaller at every parameter value.

For a large sample the leading question is whether the estimator settles on $\theta$. The [law of large numbers](prob-05-transforms-and-limits.qmd#thm-law-of-large-numbers) says that the sample mean does, and the same limit passes to continuous functions of a consistent estimator. Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent in the regular models used here.

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea
Match moments, or maximise the likelihood. Then judge the estimator by its sampling distribution: bias, variance, and the sum of the variance and the squared bias.
:::

::: {#ex-inf-normal-mle .exercise}
## Normal maximum likelihood estimates

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent and $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$, with both parameters unknown. Derive the maximum likelihood estimates of $\mu$ and of $\sigma^2$.

[Solution](#sol-inf-normal-mle)

:::

::: {#ex-inf-variance-bias .exercise}
## Bias of the two variance estimators

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be a random sample with variance $\sigma^2$, and write $s^2$ for the bias-corrected sample variance. The maximum likelihood estimator of $\sigma^2$ in the normal model is $\widehat\sigma^2=((n-1)/n)s^2$. Find the bias of $\widehat\sigma^2$, taking as known that $\E s^2=\sigma^2$.

[Solution](#sol-inf-variance-bias)

:::
